newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Pressure on Swiss franc highlights economic woes.
newsitem.headline: Pressure on Swiss franc highlights economic woes.

text.p: The Swiss franc came under heavy pressure in European trading on Tuesday, pushed down by a combination of dollar strength and concerns about the Swiss banking sector.

The franc hit a 21-month low versus the dollar at 1.2961 per dollar, before edging back to levels of about 1.2945/2955 at around 1445 GMT. It hit a 20-month low against the mark at 84.84 centimes, then crawled back to around 84.60.

"Stop loss limits at 84.40 pushed the mark up to around 84.84...we failed to clear 84.80 and this put a little bit of a damper on the move," Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) currency analyst Hans Schaerer said.
Analysts said the speculative swings were mostly caused by external factors.

But news that UBS planned to take a 3.0 billion francs special charge to cover domestic credit risks and its addition to Standard and Poor's CreditWatch list highlighted the chronically depressed condition of the Swiss economy.

"We must admit that we had underestimated how fundamentally the Swiss economy had been impacted by the ongoing process of structural change. Several sectors of industry which formerly ranked as pillars of the Swiss economy are now racked by crisis," UBS chief executive Mathis Cabiallavetta said at a news conference.
"On a psychological level I would said it does have an effect...it's as if a pillar of stability is gone," Schaerer said.
The International Monetary Fund recently forecast that the Swiss economy would contract by a real 0.5 percent this year and grow by only one percent in 1997.

UBS's steps followed more drastic plans unveiled by rivals CS Holding and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) to cope with an oversupply of retail banking in the small Swiss market and mounting loan risks after six years of virtually zero growth in the Swiss economy and a collapsed property market.

SBC in September announced a sweeping domestic restructuring including some 1,700 job cuts, or 10 percent of its Swiss workforce, and a bad loan charge of 3.3 billion Swiss francs resulting in a 1996 loss of 1.9 billion.
CS Holding said in July it was setting aside one billion Swiss francs for a global reorganisation that includes cutting 3,500 Swiss jobs plus 1,500 worldwide.
In addition, Goldman Sachs International's chief currency economist said in Tokyo earlier today that the situation in Switzerland was just as things had been in Japan 18 months ago.

The persistent strength of markets was fueling foreign interest and this in turn has led to dollar buying to the detriment of the mark and the Swiss franc, said Thomas Steinemann at Swiss Volksbank brokerage research.
In addition, he said the lira's re-entry into Europe's exchange rate mechanism was putting pressure on the mark and this was also hurting the franc. -- Zurich Editorial +41 1 631 7340
